client: I've been really struggling with work lately. After my team missed that big deadline last week, I can't stop worrying that I'm failing as a project manager. The pressure keeps building and I feel like I'm drowning in responsibilities, but I'm not sure talking about it will actually make the workload any lighter.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of responsibility and self-doubt after that missed deadline. I notice your voice sounds rushed and tense when you talk about this - would you say these worries are constantly running through your mind?  

Let's explore what "failing as a project manager" means to you - is there a specific standard you feel you're not meeting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
Yeah, I keep replaying that moment when my boss asked about the project status and I had nothing to show. I feel like a real project manager would have anticipated the delays and had backup plans. The worst part is my team looked so disappointed - that's what keeps me up at night. 

I don't know if we need to analyze what "failing" means... it's pretty obvious I dropped the ball. I just need to work harder so this never happens again.
therapist:
I hear how painful that moment with your boss and team was for you, yet your voice sounds less distressed than your words suggest - have you been trying to push these feelings aside to focus on working harder?  

You mention it's "obvious" you dropped the ball, but I wonder if there's room to consider what factors beyond your control might have contributed to the delay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know if I'm pushing feelings away exactly - it's more that I just don't have the energy to dwell on it when there's so much work piling up. But you're right that calling it "obvious" might be harsh... it's just hard not to blame myself when everyone else seemed to handle their parts fine.  

I guess some clients were slow with feedback, but shouldn't a good project manager account for that? That's literally my job. Now my boss keeps giving me these disappointed looks in meetings, and I'm terrified I'll get fired over this.
therapist:
It sounds like you're holding yourself to an extremely high standard - that a "good project manager" should anticipate every possible delay. I notice your voice speeds up when talking about this - is that pressure to be perfect adding to your exhaustion?  

When you say your boss gives you disappointed looks, what specifically makes you think those are about your performance rather than the situation as a whole?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
I know logically that no one can anticipate every delay, but I still feel like I *should* be able to. When my boss gives me that look, it's the way his eyebrows knit together and he exhales sharply—it's the exact same expression he had when another PM messed up last quarter. I can't help but think he's comparing me to that situation.  

The exhaustion is real, but what if relaxing my standards just makes me sloppy? I've seen what happens when projects go off the rails, and I don't want to be the reason for that.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between understanding intellectually that perfection isn't realistic, yet still feeling compelled to strive for it. When you mention your boss's expression, I sense a real fear of being seen as inadequate - does that comparison to the other PM feel particularly threatening to you?  

Let's explore what "relaxing your standards" would actually look like - do you think there might be a middle ground between perfection and sloppiness that could still lead to successful projects?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It does feel threatening when I compare myself to the other PM—she seems so confident and capable, and I’m always second-guessing myself. The idea of relaxing my standards makes me anxious because I worry that if I don’t push myself to be perfect, I’ll make a mistake that could ruin the project or make my boss think less of me. I’m not sure where that middle ground is—it feels like if I’m not aiming for perfection, I’m being careless.
therapist:
I hear how much pressure you're putting on yourself to measure up to this other PM's confidence, and how scary it feels to imagine your boss thinking less of you. Your voice sounds quite tense and rushed as you describe this - it seems this comparison is really weighing on you.  

What do you imagine would happen if you allowed yourself to make a small, human mistake on a project? Do you think your boss would view it differently than how you're viewing this missed deadline?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know if my boss would actually care that much about one mistake, but in my head it feels catastrophic. The thought of him seeing me as incompetent makes my chest tighten up - like all my hard work could be undone by one slip-up. 

But at the same time, I see other PMs make small errors sometimes and nobody seems to judge them harshly for it. It's confusing why I hold myself to this impossible standard.
therapist:
It's interesting that you can recognize others get grace for small mistakes, yet struggle to extend that same understanding to yourself. That "catastrophic" feeling in your chest - does it remind you of any other times in your life when you've felt this pressure to be perfect?  

You mentioned this is confusing for you - would it help to explore where these impossible standards might have come from originally?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I think it does remind me of when I was younger and my parents would get really upset over small mistakes, like if I got a B instead of an A. But I don't know if that's really connected to how I feel now. Part of me thinks I should just be able to get over it since I'm an adult now. 

The pressure feels different now though - it's like I'm the one putting it on myself, not anyone else. That almost makes it worse because I can't blame anyone but myself for feeling this way.
therapist:
It sounds like you're recognizing some patterns from your past, yet also feeling frustrated that those old experiences still affect you now. I notice your voice gets quieter and higher when talking about this - does that self-imposed pressure feel even heavier because you believe you *should* have outgrown it by now?  

You mentioned this feels different because you're the one putting pressure on yourself now - do you think part of you might still be trying to protect yourself from that old fear of disappointing others?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
Yeah, I think that's part of it. I keep telling myself I should be over this by now, but that just makes me feel worse when I'm not. It's like I'm disappointed in myself for still being affected by things that happened years ago.  

Sometimes I wonder if I'm just making excuses for myself though. Other people had tough childhoods too and they seem fine. Why can't I just move on?
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between wanting to move on from the past and feeling frustrated with yourself for still being affected by it. Your voice sounds rushed and higher-pitched as you talk about this - does that self-criticism add another layer of pressure on top of everything else?  

Rather than comparing yourself to others who seem fine, what would it look like to show yourself the same compassion you might extend to someone else in your position?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I know I should be kinder to myself, but it’s hard. Whenever I try, it just feels forced, like I’m lying to myself. I see others moving on so easily, and it makes me feel like I’m failing at something that should be simple.  

The idea of showing myself compassion sounds nice, but I don’t even know where to start. It feels like I’m just supposed to magically feel better, but I don’t.
therapist:
It makes sense that self-compassion feels forced when you're used to being so hard on yourself - these things take practice, like building any new skill. I notice your voice gets very quiet when talking about this - does that hesitation come from feeling like you "should" already have this figured out?  

What if we started small - is there one small, concrete way you could practice being gentler with yourself this week, even if it feels awkward at first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I guess my voice gets quiet because talking about self-compassion just makes me feel kind of stupid. Like why should I be nice to myself when I keep messing things up? The idea of trying some small practice makes me feel resistant—it's like a performance, you know? Like I'm pretending to care about myself when I really don't.
therapist:
I hear how uncomfortable this idea of self-compassion feels for you - like it would just be pretending or putting on an act. Your voice gets higher and faster when you talk about this, almost like there's frustration bubbling up.  

What if we reframe it not as "being nice to yourself," but simply noticing when you're being especially harsh? Would that feel any more genuine to you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
